title: Jonah and the Visitor
premise: Sable Nakamura, a pest controller who inherited their grandmother's house along with her strange trade secrets, is called to a job where the 'infestation' leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. Back home, every photograph in the house has changed: an extra chair now sits at the center of each family picture, and it is slowly pulling the people in those photos toward it. As Sable counts doors, keeps lights burning, and uncovers grandmother's ledger of things once invited in, they realize the visitor was summoned decades ago by a bargain made to save a dying child — Sable themselves. To survive until sunrise, Sable must decide whether to unmake the invitation and lose the found family that gathered around grandma's table, or let the chair be filled.
about_author: Lior Voss is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent years cataloguing the strange things people leave behind in old houses. They write horror about inheritance, domestic spaces, and the bargains families make in the dark.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Inside
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A routine call to a rental unit becomes something else when handprints appear on the inside of painted-shut windows, pressed from a room no one can open. Sable seals the room per an odd clause in grandma's old contract templates. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into personal dread — the handprints are small, like a child's.

chapters.title: The Inheritance Clause
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sorting grandma's estate, Sable finds the business ledgers: decades of jobs where the 'pest' column lists names, dates, and one recurring entry — 'the Visitor, invited [date redacted].' Emotional beat: grief interrupted by suspicion that grandma's kindness had terms attached.

chapters.title: One Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. At grandma's house, Sable notices every framed photograph now contains a plain wooden chair at its center — including pictures taken before Sable was born. The chair wasn't there yesterday. Emotional beat: quiet wrongness; the house feels like it's waiting for someone to sit down.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, intercut with neighbor Marisol's. Marisol, grandma's oldest friend, helps count the doors at dusk — eleven at noon, twelve by nightfall. Grandma's rule: never acknowledge the extra one. Emotional beat: found-family warmth strained by shared, unspoken fear.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Invitations
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Decoding grandma's cipher, Sable learns each 'job' closed an invitation — except one left deliberately open, marked with Sable's own birthdate. Emotional beat: vertigo; the horror isn't random, it's addressed to them.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Want
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. People in the photos have begun leaning toward the chair, faces blurring mid-turn. Sable burns one frame; by morning it reappears, the figures closer still. Emotional beat: futility — this thing negotiates with memory itself.

chapters.title: Marisol Remembers a Fourth Person
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She recalls childhood summers at the house with a playmate no adult would name, who always sat in the middle seat. When she says the name aloud, every light in the house dims for exactly four seconds. Emotional beat: guilt — remembering is feeding it.

chapters.title: The Client Who Isn't There
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The original caller from chapter 1 turns out to live at an address that burned down in 1998 — the same year as the redacted ledger entry. Emotional beat: the case and the house are the same case; Sable has been working one long job.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Grandma's notebook lists survival rules: keep lights on, count doors, answer nothing after midnight, never sit in the middle. Each rule is annotated with a failure and its cost. Emotional beat: grim education; grandma learned all of this the hard way.

chapters.title: Midnight Knocking
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Something knocks politely at every door in sequence, using the voices of Sable's dead mother and then, horribly, grandma herself. Sable answers nothing, hands bleeding from gripping the counter. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into discipline.

chapters.title: The Bargain Beneath the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Under the kitchen floor, Sable finds the original contract: a dying infant (Sable) saved in exchange for 'a seat at the table, forever.' The Visitor has been patient for thirty years. Emotional beat: identity shattered — Sable's whole life was collateral.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Terms
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV shifts. Marisol, Sable's coworker Dev, and teenage neighbor Priya refuse to leave, forming a vigil around Sable. The house responds by showing each of them a photograph of themselves seated in the chair, smiling. Emotional beat: love as both shield and leverage.

chapters.title: Dev Breaks a Rule
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Exhausted, Dev answers a knock at 12:01 a.m. — just to tell it to go away. The door opens onto the dining room instead of the porch. Emotional beat: dread escalating; the house now has an interior route.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The wooden chair appears physically in the hallway, dragging itself an inch closer each time someone looks away and back. Priya times it: it moves only in unobserved moments, like a weeping angel of furniture. Emotional beat: claustrophobic escalation.

chapters.title: Grandma's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A hidden page reveals grandma planned to sit in the chair herself before she died — but died first, leaving the debt unassigned. The Visitor considers debts transferable. Emotional beat: sorrow and fury entwined; even grandma's death was a default.

chapters.title: Uninviting
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Researching revocation rites, Sable attempts to formally withdraw the invitation — but revocation requires the named party to speak the words, and speaking invites conversation. The Visitor speaks first, in Sable's own voice. Emotional beat: the trap closes; language itself is the haunted ground.

chapters.title: Priya Sees It Clearly
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Youngest and least bound to the house, Priya perceives the Visitor truly: not a monster but a hollow shaped like whoever is expected, starving for a place at a table. Emotional beat: pity complicating fear — the horror is lonely too.

chapters.title: The Longest Hour
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Between 4 and 5 a.m., the house folds inward: rooms repeat, doors lead back to the dining room, the photographs show everyone already seated. Only the kitchen light holds. Emotional beat: endurance at the breaking point; sunrise as a countdown, not a promise.

chapters.title: Sitting Down
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, climax begins. Sable chooses to face the chair directly, sits in it — taking the debt into their own body rather than letting it harvest the others. The Visitor finally takes form across the table: a child-shaped absence wearing Sable's face. Emotional beat: sacrificial courage; the negotiation begins.

chapters.title: A Seat at the Table
chapters.summary: Climax. Sable offers not surrender but amendment: the Visitor may keep its seat if it stops pulling — becoming part of the household rather than its predator. Marisol sets a fifth plate. The contract rewrites itself in real ink. Emotional beat: terrifying mercy; hospitality as exorcism.

chapters.title: Sunrise Count
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Dawn comes. Doors number eleven again. The photographs show the chair occupied by a faint figure no longer reaching for anyone. Dev, Marisol, and Priya sleep in shifts; Sable keeps the lights on out of habit, not fear. Emotional beat: exhausted relief laced with vigilance.

chapters.title: What We Keep
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, epilogue. Weeks later, Sable reopens the business under new rules: some pests are invitations, and invitations can be renegotiated. A new client calls about fingerprints. At home, the fifth plate stays set. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution — identity rebuilt as chosen family, with the past permanently at the table.
